name: Esther Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential and your name won't be attached to them. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead design at Lintel Studio, a five-person agency that makes menus, shop signs and product labels for local traders. I have a master's in design, but today I spent an hour checking whether a bakery's cream colour would print the same on a window film and a paper bag. I love seeing a shopkeeper recognise their own business in a finished sign. I don't love three rounds of unpaid changes after the agreed proof.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI, and how is the work paying you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an image tool every day to test backgrounds and type combinations, then I draw and check the final artwork myself. I am the most experienced designer here, but the agency pays below what a lead designer usually earns. I rent a small flat alone, have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are only two similar studios within an easy journey. My brother lives across town, but his pay is his, not my emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our clients that a quick sketch is still only a sketch. A bakery owner pays us to get the label right on a real bag, not to produce fifty pretty guesses. I would keep showing the printer's proof beside the screen image.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My design skill should still earn a wage, but I already struggle to save on this pay. One missed invoice or a rent rise would hurt even if AI goes nowhere. I am not waiting for a machine to make that budget tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the paid label and signage work and compare each final proof with the printer's colour sample. I'd cancel the stock-image bundle I personally pay for and hardly use and put that monthly fee into an emergency account. In the first year of this mild picture I'd ask the owner for a review of my lead pay against the client accounts I manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money, not about losing the craft. I like a predictable client order, but three weeks saved is not much protection. A quiet AI year would still leave me wanting a better wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My stock-image bundle is billed to me every month even though I now draw or photograph most things myself. I'd stop that subscription and set the transfer for the same day as rent. I would not cut the colour-proof order; a bad print run costs more than the proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take work from your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. He can look over a contract if I ask, but he has his own household to run. I want the studio to pay for the responsibility I already carry.

say: I would show **printer proofs** beside screen sketches before promising a client a label.
I would tell traders a **finished sign** needs human checking.
think: I expect my **design work** to continue through mild change.
I worry **low lead pay** and three weeks saved leave little room for a rent rise.
do: Keep **paid label work** and compare final artwork with printer colour samples.
Cancel my unused **personal stock-image bundle** and transfer its monthly fee into emergency savings.
Ask the owner for a **lead-pay review** against accounts I manage.
feel: **Anxious** about existing pay and thin savings, while the craft remains useful.
S0.quote: A quiet AI year would still leave me wanting a better wage.
fieldNote: Her **craft** looks secure, but low pay and three weeks saved already worry her.
She cuts a **recurring fee** without cutting paid colour proofs.
Her daily AI use remains **routine** in this mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep paid label work and check printed colour against proofs
Cancel my personally paid stock-image subscription
Transfer my former stock-image fee into emergency savings each month
Ask agency owner to review lead pay against managed client accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner not to sell a wall of instant mock-ups as careful design. If clients want cheap variants, we should price the actual checking and print preparation separately. I would show the print shop where an automated colour choice failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Lintel could lose routine menu and label revisions, which pay for a lot of my week. My lead title will not save those hours if clients buy AI layouts directly. With three weeks saved and few local studios, a shorter paid week would hit me quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd learn the new AI preflight tool that checks bleed, fonts and image rights, using three live jobs on paid time. I'd keep taking final client proofs and give the owner a separate estimate for human print checks. If my own paid hours actually fall, I'd look at posted in-house packaging roles and compare full-week pay and hours after travel before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed enough to wake early, because I expect a large piece of paid revision work to go. I can learn a new preflight control, but that doesn't make the rent smaller. I would rather show a client what the check is worth than sell a hundred cheap drafts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different about that preflight tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The image tool I already use makes sketches; this one checks the files that go to print and flags missing font licences. I'd learn how to inspect and correct those flags on paid jobs, not just click accept. I would keep the printer's actual proof as the final test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Lintel as soon as a packaging job appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A job advert is not a wage. I'd apply after my own hours fall only if the posted duties are real, and I'd move only if a full paid week after travel covers rent, food and the rest of my bills.

say: I would ask Lintel to **price human checks** separately from automated layout variants.
I would show the **print shop** a failed automated colour choice on its proof.
think: I expect routine revisions to take a **large paid-hours cut** at Lintel.
I know **three weeks saved** and few nearby studios leave little room for a short week.
do: Learn the **new AI preflight** on three paid jobs, correcting bleed, font and rights flags.
Keep **client proofs** and give the owner a separate estimate for human print checks.
After own-hour cuts, apply to **posted packaging roles**; move only if full-week pay and hours after travel cover rent, food and bills.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost paid revision hours and thin savings.
S1.quote: A job advert is not a wage.
fieldNote: She expects a **large paid cut**, despite being a top designer.
New preflight learning is distinct from her **daily sketch tool**.

steps.text: Learn new AI print-preflight controls on three paid client jobs
Keep checking client printer proofs and price that work separately
Apply for posted packaging after hour cuts; move for rent/food/bill-covering weekly wages and hours after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shopkeepers that cheap AGI artwork by 2028 may arrive before anyone can judge what happens to their printed products. Robots around 2031 are later; they do nothing for a studio whose work is already on a screen. I would ask each client what they still need checked in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Lintel to lose most layout fees in the first year after 2028, maybe enough to close the design desk. My master's and good eye won't create a paid order by themselves. Three weeks saved is barely a search, so I need to protect current pay while I find another route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask our three repeat clients whether they would pay for on-site proof and installation checks, and get written prices for that work. I'd keep every paid design order while it exists and stop buying speculative software subscriptions. If the design desk closes in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for posted paid print-production jobs; I would take one only after seeing the weekly wage, hours, travel cost and actual machine duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and I would sleep badly if orders started falling. I have a plan to test real print work, but not enough cash to bluff my way through months of empty promises. The later robots might reach that work too, so I won't call it permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a printing course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would visit the print shop to learn what its operator actually does, but I cannot pay a course fee or lose a paid day for a role that is not posted. If a print employer requires a short course for a posted paid vacancy and covers the fee and the missed wages, I would take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the repeat clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether they would pay for me to check a mounted sign or a first print run in person. If they only want a free visit, it will not replace a design fee. A promise of exposure does not pay my landlord.

say: I would warn clients that **2028 thinking AI** reaches design screens before later robots.
I would ask what **paid physical checks** clients still value.
think: I expect most **layout fees** to disappear, possibly closing Lintel’s design desk.
I cannot fund a long search with **three weeks saved**.
do: Ask three **repeat clients** for paid on-site proof rates while keeping design orders.
Stop **buying speculative software**; after 2028 closure, apply to posted print roles, taking only after checking wages, hours, travel, duties.
Take a **required print course** only for a posted paid vacancy with fee and missed wages covered.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost fees and a search window measured in weeks.
S2.quote: A promise of exposure does not pay my landlord.
fieldNote: The **2028 loss** reaches her screen-based design before physical print work.
She tests paid client demand rather than assuming visits **replace fees**.
A required course needs a **posted paid vacancy**, covered fee and covered missed wages.

steps.text: Keep paid design orders and ask three clients for paid on-site proof rates
Stop buying new speculative software subscriptions before design fees fall
After 2028 closure, apply for posted print roles; check weekly wages, hours, travel, duties before taking
Take required print course only for posted paid vacancy with fee and missed wages covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team five years lets us build a body of printed work while clients still pay us. I would like a shopfront painter to show me why some lettering survives rain and some peels. Thinking AI can make a sign image by 2031; robots around 2034 may later change fitting and painting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could develop a small run of hand-painted signs without buying a workshop, but I cannot assume people will pay my rate. My current design wage is low, yet it is still the rent. Five years gives me time to prove demand before I shift it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd offer two existing clients a priced, hand-painted window-lettering trial, with materials paid in the quote before I order paint. I'd keep my agency hours and record real receipts and time on each job. In the first year after 2031, if Lintel's design orders end, I'd seek a posted paid sign-production role unless repeat paid lettering orders already cover my rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a test I can afford. I would be proud to hand over a finished window rather than a file, though I know robots may come for installation later. I would not spend rent money on brushes to look brave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if those two clients say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the trial stops there. I'd keep paid agency work while it exists and check posted sign-production hours rather than buy materials for an imaginary queue. My three weeks saved are for rent gaps, not a showroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paid sign shop job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the actual weekly pay and hours after travel meet rent and bills, or the paid lettering receipts really close the difference. I would ask what lifting and ladder work is involved before accepting a shift. I can paint well; I have not been trained to fit a high sign alone.

say: I would use five years to test **paid physical lettering**, not only produce screen images.
I would tell clients **2031 thinking AI** arrives before fitting robots around 2034.
think: I see hand lettering as a **possible paid path**, not proven demand.
I still need my **agency wage** while the trial is small.
do: Quote two **window-lettering trials** with materials prepaid; if both decline, keep agency work and inspect posted sign roles.
Keep **paid agency hours**, record lettering receipts; after 2031 order loss, seek posted sign work unless lettering covers rent/bills.
Accept **sign work** only if after-travel weekly wages/hours cover rent/bills or paid lettering closes the gap; ask about lifting/ladders.
feel: **Anxious**, with an affordable test but no proven replacement wage.
S3.quote: I would not spend rent money on brushes to look brave.
fieldNote: A **paid two-client test** precedes any claim that physical work replaces design fees.
Her printer and sign contacts offer a path, but **2034 robots** remain a risk.
She asks about **lifting and ladders** before accepting sign work.

steps.text: Quote two clients for window letters with materials paid before purchase
Keep paid agency hours and log lettering receipts and working time
If both clients decline now, inspect posted sign-production roles
After 2031 loss, accept posted work only with rent/bill-covering after-travel wages/hours or paid lettering; check lifting/ladders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young designer ten years is enough to build clients who trust the finished object, not just an image. I would still use tools, but I would keep a folder of signs that lasted through weather and reprints. AGI by 2036 can do the desk artwork; robots around 2039 may later tackle more fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could make a living from production and client trust by then, but I have no guarantee and very little money now. I don't want to leave paid work in 2026 for a story about 2036. A decade only helps if the first few years improve my cash cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd raise my emergency balance from three weeks toward three months using paid lead-design and lettering receipts. Each spring I'd compare local posted print and sign wages with my actual agency income. In the first year after 2036, if paid design orders end, I'd take a posted production role only if its full-week wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills; otherwise I'd keep any paid agency orders and the lettering clients while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end point, but I can make useful decisions before then. My own income looks secure for the next few years if I keep client work and build the reserve. I would feel foolish if I mistook a ten-year warning for ten years of guaranteed work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the agency earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real paid production offer with a workable week, not a promise that printing will survive every robot. I would look at the wage and hours after travel and ask about the lifting before I accepted. If the offer is worse than the rent, I stay with paid orders and keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother help with the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might give me advice about a contract, but my brother has his own bills. I would build the reserve from my work, not count his account as mine. Ten years cannot be lived on someone else's promise.

say: I would tell young designers to build **finished-work evidence** alongside digital images.
I would explain **2036 desk AGI** arrives before more capable fitting robots.
think: I see **production and client trust** as possible income, without assuming it lasts.
I need a **larger cash cushion** before the long warning helps.
do: Build **emergency savings** from three weeks toward three months using paid work.
Compare **print and sign wages** each spring with actual agency income.
After 2036 order loss, take **posted production work** only on rent/bill-covering full-week wages/hours after travel; otherwise keep paid agency and lettering orders.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2036, while her own near-term client income looks secure.
S4.quote: I would feel foolish if I mistook a ten-year warning for ten years of guaranteed work.
fieldNote: She does not count **family money** as her reserve.
The **production path** still faces later robots and has to pay a real week.
Her near-term own income looks **secure**, unlike in the faster scenarios.

steps.text: Grow emergency savings from three weeks toward three months using paid design and lettering receipts
Compare posted print/sign wages each spring; after 2036 closure, take rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel
Keep paid agency orders and lettering clients during any 2036 search

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our screen fees might go before I have saved enough for a search. I need real paid work at a print shop, or clients willing to pay for physical checks, not another glossy course advert. Three weeks of rent money is a poor bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the print proofs when everyone wants a cheap image. A wrong label is a loss for the baker and the printer as well as the designer. My master's taught me to make decisions, not to call every sketch a finished job.

headlineQuote: Three weeks of rent money is a poor bridge.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old lead designer** with a master’s degree at a five-person agency serving local traders.
She uses AI **daily**, yet checks printed colour and rights herself.
Low lead pay, **three weeks saved** and few nearby studios make lost design fees urgent.
She tests **paid physical lettering** without buying materials before clients cover them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase screen fees before she can build a search reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A **real paid print role** or clients paying for physical proof checks.
